For the teachers of India, the nation builders

A teacher shapes how a generation meets AI.

That's you. You don't need to have it all figured out. In just a few minutes, GuruSutr-AI gives you a quick starting point on where you are with AI, helps build real confidence, and points you toward practical ways to bring it into your classroom, in six Indian languages.

A way to think about it, not one more thing to learn

Teacher decides. AI helps build.

GuruSutr-AI keeps saying teachers should bring AI into the classroom. This page is the part that was missing: how. Decide what you want your students to think or do first. Then see if AI can help you get there faster, not the other way around.

To make this concrete, everything below follows one real theme already in Classroom exercises: Saving Water. The same three class groups you will see there show how one resource can be taught at a growing depth of thinking, with AI helping at every stage, never deciding what the stage should be.

Decide what you want your students to think or do. Then bring in AI to help you build it. Not the other way around.

This uses one theme, Water, to make the idea concrete. Most class groups blend more than one kind of thinking, this is not a strict rule of one level per class. Everything here starts from Class 3, roughly the earliest stage where students begin using AI tools themselves.

Classes 3 to 5

Mostly Apply: using a skill like measuring or recording for a real purpose.

FROM CLASSROOM EXERCISES

Bucket vs. running tap measurement. Measure how much water a bucket bath uses compared to a 5 minute running shower, using a measuring jug.

Teacher decides

What skill is being practiced, here it is measurement with a reason, and how precise it needs to be.

AI may support

Generate a simple recording sheet, or one more comparison at the same difficulty.

Classes 6 to 8

Mostly Analyze and Create: drawing connections, then building something new from them.

FROM CLASSROOM EXERCISES

Design a rainwater harvesting model. Sketch a simple rainwater harvesting system for your rooftop, labeling each part and its purpose.

Teacher decides

What the design brief requires, and what a finished answer should show.

AI may support

Explain one technical part a student is stuck on, or suggest design ideas to brainstorm from.

Classes 9 to 12

Mostly Evaluate, and still Create: judging what is worth doing, then proposing something real.

FROM CLASSROOM EXERCISES

Cost benefit analysis of a rainwater harvesting system. Estimate the installation cost of a basic rooftop harvesting system against annual water savings, and decide if it is worth it.

Teacher decides

What worth it means for this exercise, cost, water saved, or something else entirely.

AI may support

Help calculate once the numbers are given, or argue the opposite case so the student's conclusion gets tested.

Where this goes next

By Classes 9 to 12, a student who has spent years auditing the school's water use has a real question in front of them: is this also a job? Vocational pathways already connects Water and gardening to a genuine career route, agricultural extension and irrigation work through Krishi Vigyan Kendras. The same thread that started with a leaking tap in Classes 3 to 5 can end in an honest career conversation ten years later.

Teachers already showing the way

Every story here is a real, named programme or person, with a public source you can check. Nothing on this page is invented, combined from different stories, or presented as bigger than what was reported. If a story cannot be sourced, it does not go here. It belongs among the practice ideas elsewhere on this site.

Karnataka: AI drafts, teachers decide

The challenge: Teachers spend significant time creating bilingual lesson plans aligned to the curriculum, along with activities and records. That is time that comes out of preparing for the students in front of them.

What happened: Shiksha Copilot, built by Microsoft Research India with the Sikshana Foundation, was rolled out to 1,043 teachers across 757 schools in Karnataka between December 2024 and March 2025, for Grades 5 to 10, in English and Kannada. The tool generates a first draft of a lesson plan; teachers review it and adapt it for their own classroom.

What was measured: Teachers reported saving roughly two hours a week on planning, and a stress score teachers reported themselves fell from a median of 4.25 to 3.25 on a 7 point scale. Teachers also used the tool to keep records and generate assessments, not just lesson plans.

The lesson: AI can help with the first draft. The teacher decides what will actually work for a particular class, language level, and learning need.

Source: Microsoft Research India and the Sikshana Foundation's published deployment study on this rollout (arXiv:2507.00456); Microsoft Source Asia feature.

Andhra Pradesh: one teacher, tools built for his own students

The challenge: Students in rural schools with limited resources often have fewer opportunities for personalised support and digital learning resources outside class.

What happened: Rajesh Kouluri, a teacher at MPPS Chinamallupeta in Vizianagaram district, Andhra Pradesh, built "RajClassroom" (lessons, videos and games in Telugu, English and Maths) and "Hello Dhriti," an app powered by AI with voice recognition and gamified lessons aligned to NEP 2020. Hello Dhriti has reached more than 15,700 students across 2,574 schools; RajClassroom and his other resources have reached far more teachers and students across the state.

What was recognised: Kouluri was named one of 48 teachers to receive the National Teachers' Award 2026, presented by President Droupadi Murmu on 5 September 2026.

The lesson: AI does not need to be reserved for urban schools that already have more funding. A single motivated teacher, with the right tools and content in the local language, can widen access to quality learning.

Source: National Teachers' Award 2026, Ministry of Education, Government of India; reported by The Logical Indian.

For the teachers of India, the nation builders

About GuruSutr-AI

AI is already entering students’ lives. They are using it to search, write, translate, prepare projects and find answers in seconds.

The important question is not whether students will use AI. They will. The question is: who will help them use it well?

That role belongs to the teacher.

India has more than one crore teachers. Every day, they work with students who have different languages, abilities, aspirations and access to technology. Some teach large classrooms. Some support first generation learners. Some are already experimenting with digital tools. Many are still trying to understand what AI means for their subject, their students and their own role.

GuruSutr-AI is created for them.

It is a simple space to help teachers understand AI without jargon or fear. AI can help with a worksheet, a lesson idea, or a set of practice questions. But it cannot understand a child’s confidence, home situation, learning gap or potential in the way a teacher can.

That is why teachers matter even more now.

GuruSutr-AI helps teachers, students and families explore AI in a practical and responsible way. It also encourages schools to look beyond marks alone. Young people need academic learning, but they also need hands on skills, communication, digital awareness, vocational exposure and confidence to work in a changing world.

Available in English, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali and Marathi, GuruSutr-AI aims to make this conversation accessible to more people across India.

AI can give students answers. Teachers can help them make sense of them.

Start with a short reflection, then explore practical classroom ideas.

Why I built this

AI is already in our classrooms, ready or not. I spent 17 years in HR and Strategy across corporates. Children and the way they are educated matter to me, especially those from underprivileged backgrounds. I support NGOs working in education. I am also a trained Yoga teacher and Yoga Nidra Facilitator, and I love working with kids and want to do my bit in creating a better world for them.

So I built GuruSutr-AI. A free, simple way for teachers to check where they stand with AI, and find a few practical next steps.

It is still small. Still growing. Built in case it helps even one teacher.

On the product

I used Claude Sonnet mostly to build it. The core idea was how to improve AI literacy among teachers through approved resources, and how this can be integrated into education, and what role vocational training is going to play in the future given AI reshapes the world of work.

Varsha Vijayaraghavan

From classrooms around the world

Six things thoughtful AI era teaching has in common

Nobody knows how fast AI will change teaching. What matters is what you do now, with what you already have. That is a real responsibility. You do not need to have every answer to begin thoughtfully.

One teacher, many paths

AI can create practice at different levels, explain an idea in a different way, or provide a first pass translation for a student who needs support. You still check the quality and decide who needs what.

Where could one student take a different path than the rest, starting this week?

How about just one student, this week? See how it goes.

AI can be a thinking partner, not an answer machine

The habit that matters most is not a clever prompt. It is checking what AI says. Ask AI, check the answer against a trusted source, a class text, data, or your own judgment, then explain it back in your own words. If a student cannot do that last step, they may not have learned it yet.

Think of one moment this week where a student could check an AI answer instead of just accepting it.

Try it on one lesson this week. What do you think?

Evidence of learning is becoming more important

A finished page has never been the whole story about understanding. With AI, it helps to also look at how a student arrived at the answer, a short conversation, a voice note, a diagram, or comparing an early draft with the final version. This is not a rule, just something worth trying.

Is there one assignment where students could show more of their process?

Add it to just one assignment. See how it feels.

Let AI carry your paperwork, not your classroom

If you have never used AI, start here. Let it create a first draft of a lesson plan, a rubric, or a parent email. Then review it for accuracy and fit for your students. It saves you time for the parts of teaching AI cannot do.

What's the one task eating your time that this could take off your plate first?

Hand off just one task this week. See if it helps.

Keep your students safe while they explore

For younger students especially, consider keeping AI use supervised, and use only tools your school or district has approved. Never put a student's name, photo, schoolwork, or other personal details into an unapproved tool. One habit covers most of this: before using any new tool, ask what data it collects, where that data goes, and who can see it.

How could you make one safety habit really stick with your students, not just mention it once?

Say it once more, out loud, this week. That's enough to start.

This works whether you use AI a lot or not at all

Some teachers use AI every day. Some barely use it. Both are fine starting points. What matters is whether your students are learning to think, with it or without it.

Where are you starting from today? That is a fine place to be.

Wherever that is, it's enough for today.

Drawn from Stanford's 2026 K to 12 AI research review, OECD's 2026 reporting on generative AI in schools, and UNESCO's guidance on age appropriate, human centered AI in education.

For students in the age of AI

Ten future skills, five buckets you can actually teach

Class 3 and Class 12 do not learn the same way, so here is one classroom activity per bucket for each class group, not a long repeated list. Pick the one that fits the students in front of you.

Think

Employer surveys from the World Economic Forum name analytical thinking as the single most wanted skill, and it costs nothing to build. It just means asking a student to question a claim instead of accepting it.

Classes 3 to 5

Spot the claim. Find one claim in an ad or poster and ask together: how do we know this is true?

Classes 6 to 8

Claim Detective. Check one online or AI generated claim using two credible sources.

Classes 9 to 12

Evidence Brief. Take a claim people are currently debating, like whether AI will remove all jobs, and write a short, evidence based view with real sources.

Can the student explain why they believe this?

Try it on one claim this week, not a whole unit.

Use AI wisely

This bucket is simple: using AI is not the skill. Checking it is.

Classes 3 to 5

Spot the mistake. Show an AI generated answer with one deliberate error, and have students find it using their textbook.

Classes 6 to 8

AI Answer Audit. Ask AI to explain a lesson topic, check three facts, and rewrite the answer in your own words.

Classes 9 to 12

AI Use Statement. Use AI for a research or project draft, fact check the key points, and submit the prompts used, the sources checked, and the final revised work.

Can the student use a tool, verify it, and use it responsibly?

Swap in whatever topic you're already teaching this week.

Connect

Communication and empathy appear in every major global skills framework as their own category, not as an extra add on.

Classes 3 to 5

Ask and listen. Ask someone at home what makes them feel happy or safe at school, then draw or write their answer.

Classes 6 to 8

Listen Before You Solve. In groups, interview three people about one school issue and suggest one realistic change.

Classes 9 to 12

Stakeholder Project. Interview people who see a local issue differently from each other, and present a balanced recommendation.

Can the student work with and explain ideas to others?

Three conversations are enough. It does not need to be bigger.

Grow

Skills do not last as long as they used to. What lasts is a habit: noticing you are stuck, asking for feedback, and adjusting.

Classes 3 to 5

Seven day practice. Choose one small skill and keep track of practicing it for a week.

Classes 6 to 8

Learning Sprint. Practise one challenging skill for 10 to 14 days, get feedback twice, and show what changed.

Classes 9 to 12

Improve a Draft. Submit a first version of a speech, project, or presentation, ask for feedback, then submit an improved version with a short reflection.

Can the student improve after feedback or failure?

Pick one student to try this with first, see how it goes.

Create value

This is not only about starting a business. It is about noticing a real problem and doing something about it. That is the same instinct behind a good local project and a good startup.

Classes 3 to 5

Make a helpful reminder. Create a poster or sticker about saving water, switching off lights, or keeping the classroom clean.

Classes 6 to 8

Small Local Solution. Create a checklist, poster, survey, or guide for a real school problem, and test it with two people.

Classes 9 to 12

Community Micro Project. Identify a local need, speak with the people affected by it, create a small solution, test it, revise it, and present what happened.

Can the student identify a real need and act responsibly?

Even a checklist counts as a solution here.

Extra resources, not another bucket
Project themes worth trying

Any of these work across class groups, just adjust the depth. None of them require anything beyond what most schools already have.

Saving water at school or at home Reducing plastic and sorting waste Road safety near school Spotting digital payment and OTP scams Healthy tiffins and reducing food waste Respecting local occupations and the people who do skilled work Learning about different careers A bilingual guide for parents, grandparents, or younger children Saving energy: lights, fans, ACs, and chargers Helping older adults feel confident with smartphones or online services
A simple way to spread this across five weeks

You do not have to teach all five buckets in one week. Here is one simple way to spread it out, one bucket at a time:

  • Week 1, Think: check one claim
  • Week 2, Use AI wisely: spot one AI mistake
  • Week 3, Connect: ask and listen to one person
  • Week 4, Grow: practise one skill and get feedback
  • Week 5, Create value: make one useful thing

By the end, a student has five small pieces of work, a kind of Future Skills Portfolio, showing how they think, use technology carefully, work with people, improve, and solve problems.

Where this comes from

Drawn from the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs analysis of fastest growing skills, the OECD Learning Compass 2030's framework of transformative competencies, and India's National Curriculum Framework 2023 on communication and multilingualism.

Skilled trades and career routes

Work AI is changing, and the practical skills that still matter

For years, vocational learning was seen as the path for students who were not "academic enough." India's NEP 2020 points the other way: it proposes that every student in Grades 6 to 8 get hands on exposure to real crafts like carpentry, electrical work, metal work, gardening, and pottery, shaped by local needs, though how fully this reaches every school still varies. Germany and Switzerland treat vocational routes as a first choice, not a fallback. In the US, AI is reshaping many desk based tasks quickly, and a 2026 Randstad USA analysis of job postings found demand for skilled trades growing three times faster than for professional roles between 2022 and 2026, a US finding, not a global or India wide one, but a sign that hands on work is changing, not disappearing.

Here are seven everyday themes. Each one has a classroom activity for every class group, so pick the one that fits the students in front of you.

Want many more activities on water, energy, or digital safety specifically? See Classroom exercises above, it has 38 civic and life skill activities per topic, not career focused like these.

🛡 Keeping students safe, always (Refer to the school guidelines)

Field work: an adult goes along for interviews, visits, and any tool use.

Online: never share an OTP, PIN, or password; never post home, family, or uniform photos.

With people: stay in public places, go in pairs, and ask before taking a photo.

Food and nutrition
Classes 3 to 5

Draw the journey of a meal, from farm to home.

Classes 6 to 8

Plan a healthy, low cost tiffin and work out the ingredient costs.

Classes 9 to 12

Interview a food business owner or farmer and create a simple cost, waste, and marketing plan.

REAL WORLD SCENARIO

A small tiffin service owner gets an order for 50 lunches by tomorrow morning, but the vegetable vendor delivers late and one ingredient is missing. What would you check or change first?

Vocational Training Route: food production and hospitality skills can be learned through ITIs where available, skill centres, and hotel management or food production diploma courses. Many small food businesses start informally and later register under FSSAI food safety rules, with some able to access support through PMFME, the government's scheme for micro food processing enterprises.

Can the student connect what they eat to the work behind it?

One meal, traced back. That's the whole activity.

Water and gardening
Classes 3 to 5

Plant a seed and keep a growth diary.

Classes 6 to 8

Build a simple compost bin or a water saving project.

Classes 9 to 12

Run a school water audit and propose one low cost fix.

REAL WORLD SCENARIO

A farmer's borewell is running dry earlier every summer, and the local Krishi Vigyan Kendra suggests drip irrigation, but it costs money upfront. What would the farmer want to know before deciding?

Vocational Training Route: Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs), part of ICAR's nationwide agricultural extension network, train farmers and students in irrigation and modern farming methods in many locations. Agricultural extension and irrigation work is a real career path connected to this training.

SAFETY NOTE

Use only safe household or school materials, avoid sharp tools, and wash hands after handling soil or compost.

Can the student notice where a resource is used, wasted, or saved?

Start with one tap or one plant, not the whole school.

Repair and maintenance
Classes 3 to 5

Name the tools used at home and what each one is safely for.

Classes 6 to 8

Learn basic tool safety and watch a real repair happen.

Classes 9 to 12

Interview an electrician, mechanic, or technician about how smart tools or digital diagnostics have changed their work.

REAL WORLD SCENARIO

A ceiling fan stops working, and two people in the house guess different reasons why. How would a trained electrician safely work out what is actually wrong before deciding on a repair?

Vocational Training Route: electrician, fitter, and related trades are widely taught at ITIs, commonly running one to two years depending on the trade. Graduates may also apply for apprenticeship openings supported through the National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme, subject to employer availability.

SAFETY NOTE

Students should not handle electrical tools, open appliances, or attempt repairs themselves. Keep this to observation and safety awareness, with any real repair done by a supervised, qualified adult.

Can the student explain how a trade is changing, not just what it is?

The "what changed" question is more interesting than "what do you do."

Local crafts and business
Classes 3 to 5

Draw or describe a local craft you've seen someone make.

Classes 6 to 8

Meet a craftsperson and try making a small item, or make a poster about their work.

Classes 9 to 12

Create a simple online selling idea for a local artisan, without posting anyone's personal details.

REAL WORLD SCENARIO

A weaver has loyal local customers but wants to sell to buyers in other cities. What would she need to work out first, packaging, pricing, or shipping?

Vocational Training Route: PM Vishwakarma Yojana, a central government scheme launched in 2023, gives traditional artisans and craftspeople skill training, a toolkit incentive, and collateral free loans to grow exactly this kind of business.

Can the student see a craft as a business, not just a skill?

A poster, product label, or customer story can be a first step in understanding how a craft reaches people.

Carpentry and metal work
Classes 3 to 5

Look at wooden and metal things around you, a chair, a gate, a bucket, and guess how each one was made.

Classes 6 to 8

Watch a carpenter or a metal worker at work, and list the tools they use safely.

Classes 9 to 12

Interview a carpenter, welder, or metal worker about how new tools or machines have changed their work.

REAL WORLD SCENARIO

A customer asks a carpenter to build a bookshelf into an odd shaped corner, but the wall isn't quite straight. What would the carpenter need to measure or plan around first?

Vocational Training Route: carpentry, welding, and fitter trades are taught at ITIs across India, and skilled workers can move into supervisory or contracting roles after a few years of on the job experience.

Can the student see the skill behind an ordinary object?

Start with just one object in the room.

Digital safety and services
Classes 3 to 5

Learn the rule: never share a password or an OTP with anyone.

Classes 6 to 8

Make a scam awareness poster for families at home.

Classes 9 to 12

Run a short digital safety session for parents or older adults on OTP fraud and scams.

REAL WORLD SCENARIO

An elderly neighbor gets a call saying their bank account will be blocked unless they share an OTP right now. What should they do in that exact moment?

Vocational Training Route: basic IT support and digital literacy training is offered through short courses under PMKVY (Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana) and other state skill programmes, though availability and quality vary by location.

SAFETY NOTE

If this happens: do not share the OTP, PIN, password, card number, or screen access. End the call, and check the account only through the bank's official app or the number printed on the card. To report a loss, call India's cybercrime helpline, 1930, or use the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. For younger students, the lesson is simpler: tell a trusted adult immediately.

Can the student protect someone else, not just themselves?

Grandparents and parents are the real audience here, not classmates.

Energy and sustainability
Classes 3 to 5

Make a reminder poster: switch off lights and fans when you leave a room.

Classes 6 to 8

Track when lights, fans, projectors, or charging points are left on for one week.

Classes 9 to 12

Look into solar energy as a career path, and estimate the savings from one energy idea.

REAL WORLD SCENARIO

A shop owner's electricity bill keeps rising, and a salesperson suggests switching to solar panels. What would the shop owner need to calculate before deciding?

Vocational Training Route: Suryamitra is a National Institute of Solar Energy programme that trains people for solar panel installation, operation, and maintenance roles, relevant as India expands its renewable energy capacity.

Can the student turn a habit into a number?

One week of tracking is enough to make the point.

Extra resources, not another theme
A Skill Around Us: one project for any class

Every student already knows someone worth learning from, a driver, tailor, nurse, farmer, or shopkeeper, someone in their own family or street. Send them off with three questions.

What problem does this work solve?

What skills does it take?

What is changing about it right now?

That is the whole project. No two students will bring back the same story.

What they turn in:

Classes 3 to 5

A drawing and three sentences.

Classes 6 to 8

A one page profile, told out loud in two minutes.

Classes 9 to 12

A full "Career Reality Card," like a short biography of a job.

Your role in this

You do not need to know a trade. You just need to open the door to it.

  • Connect one lesson to real work: fractions through tailoring, science through solar panels, language through an interview
  • Bring in one local worker for twenty minutes. That is often enough
  • Call out the dignity in it: every job takes real skill and judgement, even the ones we walk past every day
  • Mix up who tries what. Repair, cooking, and budgeting are not "for" one gender
  • Every path counts: ITI, apprenticeship, degree, or starting a business
  • Let AI help you prepare, not replace the interview itself
Where this comes from

Randstad, 2026: analysis of over 150 million US job postings found skilled trade demand growing roughly three times faster than professional roles, with especially rapid growth in robotics technicians, HVAC, industrial automation, construction, electricians, and welders. This is US evidence of the AI infrastructure effect, not India specific labour data. World Economic Forum, Future of Jobs Report 2025: technology, the green transition, and demographic shifts are reshaping jobs and skills worldwide, alongside analytical thinking, creativity, resilience, and technological literacy. OECD on Switzerland and Germany: vocational education is a mainstream, respected route in both countries, not a fallback. India's NEP 2020 calls for all Grades 6 to 8 students to get hands on exposure to vocational crafts, including carpentry, electrical work, metal work, gardening, and pottery, alongside local vocational experts. India's PM Vishwakarma Yojana formally supports traditional artisans and craftspeople. UNESCO's TVET Strategy 2022 to 2029 positions vocational education as essential for employment, entrepreneurship, sustainability, and lifelong learning.
